catalog_locator: Thesis p. 51, §1.8 'El acento' in ch. II 'La lengua de Pajapan'; stress shift: p. 71 §32612; demonstratives always stressed: p. 75 §3338; clitics never stressed: p. 76 §34; clause accent: p. 80 §42; 'El acento también tiene valor fonémico': p. 47.
catalog_quote: [p. 51] 1.8. El acento recae por lo general en la penúltima sílaba. En nuestro material sólo lo hemos marcado cuando recae en otras sílabas. Lo hemos considerado fonémico porque establece cambios de significado: aya "todavía", ayá "ya no"; ga:wa "deja", gawáh "caballo". [p. 71, §32612, on the suffix -skia "acción incompleta frustrada"] Cuando aparece con uno de los alternantes del sufijo plural de tercer orden: -h, el acento se desplaza a la última sílaba. Ejemplo: goniskiáh "lo tomarían". [p. 75, §3338] Algunas partículas demostrativas son: hi:n "éste", ho:n "ese", "aquel"; que son siempre acentuadas, aún en combianciones [sic] como: ihkí:n "así de esta manera", ihkó:n "así de esa manera", bagí:n "fue en esto cuando..", bagó:n "en ese entonces" (bak "cuando.."). [p. 76, §34] Los clíticos no se acentúan nunca, y por su caracter dependiente no los hemos considerado como una gran clase aparte, sino ligada casi siempre a la de los verbos. También hemos considerado que las expresiones Nombre/Verbo/Partícula + Clítico recaen dentro del nivel de palabra; aunque por razones prácticas no los hemos incluido en las fórmulas.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Lo hemos considerado fonémico porque establece cambios de significado: aya "todavía", ayá "ya no"; ga:wa "deja", gawáh "caballo". 2. Patrón silábico. [...] [verb morphology:] ... new_statements.translation: Stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable. In our material we have marked it only when it falls on other syllables. We have considered it phonemic because it produces changes of meaning: aya 'still', ayá 'no longer'; ga:wa 'leave (it)', gawáh 'horse'. 2. Syllable pattern. [...] [verb morphology:] ... the stress shifts to the last syllable. Example: goniskiáh 'they would take it if they could'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate; a residue of words (some adverbs, loans like gawáh 'horse', and certain inflected verb forms where a suffix attracts/shifts stress to the final syllable) have final stress, which the author writes with an acute accent and treats as phonemically contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on word-level secondary stress in the snippets; at clause level the author says each clause has one primary accent and one or more secondary accents, the primary accent almost always on the last word of the clause ('El acento primario casi siempre recae en la última palabra..').
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs aya/ayá, ga:wa/gawáh with final stress; stress shifts to the final syllable in certain verb forms (example goniskiáh 'lo tomarían si pudieran', tied to a verbal suffix discussed at §3261x). A 1984 SMA Mesa Redonda paper summarises: 'En Pajapan, es normalmente grave' (normally penultimate) while calling Nahua accent 'émico' in most dialects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from the phonology chapter (citation/lexical forms); separate clause-level statement places primary clause accent on the last word depending on final intonation contour.
new_statements.identity_note: García de León 1976 describes the speech of the municipio of Pajapan, Veracruz = Glottolog isth1241 / ISO nhp exactly (WALS 'Nahuatl (Pajapan)', code npa, is based on the same book). Do not substitute Wolgemuth's Mecayapan-Tatahuicapan grammar (isth1242, nhx), which only notes that Pajapan is 'muy parecido'. García de León's 1968 Tlalocan texts are from Zaragoza and Jáltipan, not Pajapan.

new_statements.translation: [p. 51, §1.8] Stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable. In our material we have marked it only when it falls on other syllables. We have considered it phonemic because it produces changes of meaning: aya 'still', ayá 'no longer'; ga:wa 'leaves', gawáh 'horse'. [p. 47] Stress also has phonemic value. [p. 71, §32612, on -skia] When it appears with one of the alternants of the third-order plural suffix, -h, the stress shifts to the last syllable. Example: goniskiáh 'they would take it'. [p. 76, §34] Clitics are never stressed

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penult, penultimate stress) and as the existing 1976 statement; the §1.8 wording is identical to the 1976 book's paragraph, so this thesis is its source and supplies the page the existing statement lacked (thesis p. 51). It adds: stress is treated as phonemic with marked exceptions; the -skia + -h shift to final; the stress behaviour of particles and clitics; clause-level primary/secondary accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress on the word; the author marks stress only where it falls elsewhere and treats it as phonemic because of minimal pairs (aya/ayá; ga:wa/gawáh, the latter a Spanish loan with final stress). Morphological exception: a verb in -skia takes final stress when the plural -h is added (goniskiáh). Particles/clitics: the negative prefix a- is always unstressed (p. 73 §331), demonstrative particles hi:n, ho:n are always stressed even in compounds ihkí:n, ihkó:n, bagí:n, bagó:n (p. 75 §3338), and the five clitics (mawix=, =ya, =wach, =gok, =san) are never stressed (p. 76 §34).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on word-level secondary stress. Clause level only (p. 80, §42): 'Cada cláusula tiene un acento primario y uno o más acentos secundarios. El acento primario casi siempre recae en la última palabra; sobre todo cuando la cláusula se halla en el final de una oración con cadencia final de tono medio o ascendente. Cuando esta entonación final es descendente, el acento primario se halla en la penúltima palabra.'
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked non-penult stress (ayá 'ya no', gawáh 'caballo', awél 'imposible', ayéh 'no es', aiká 'ya no'); final stress on -skia verbs with plural -h (goniskiáh); always-stressed demonstrative particles hi:n/ho:n and their compounds; never-stressed clitics and the atonic negative prefix a-.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis (title page: 'PAJAPAN - Una Variante del Nahua de Este -', ENAH, México D.F., 1969, Antonio García de León Griego) describes the Nahua spoken in Pajapan, Veracruz, from the author's own fieldwork; this is the same variety as the catalog's 'Nahua de Pajapan' (isth1241, ISO nhp). The text calls it 'el nahua de Pajapan' (p. 80, §421).
